extracted.intended_audience: Army/DoD contracting and oversight officials, TRADOC and installation commanders, congressional oversight staff
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and criteria for evaluating and administering an OMB Circular A-76 logistics contract (cost comparisons, award-fee design, productivity measurement, internal controls, and oversight) such as the Ft. Sill logistics contract.

rubrics_metrics.name: OMB Circular A-76 requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Office of Management and Budget Circular A-76 requires Federal agencies to: determine what commercial activities can be done more economically by private contractors than by Government employees; conduct a management study to determine how the in-house workforce should be organized and equipped to do the work most efficiently and develop a performance work statement; prepare a document containing the Government’s estimate of the lowest number and types of employees required to do the work described in the work statement; and compare the Government estimate to contractor bids to determine which alternative is more cost-effective. Inherently Governmental functions are to continue to be done by Federal employees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These steps form the procedural and substantive framework for deciding whether to convert work to contract performance and for establishing the in-house minimum requirement used as the performance baseline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contract award decision rule (cost comparison)
rubrics_metrics.description: A contract is to be awarded if the total projected cost to contract out is less than the Government estimate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cost comparisons should be based on comparable criteria for both in-house and contractor alternatives; variables include differing labor wage rates and contract administration fees. The Appeals Board adjustments to initial estimates should be reflected in the decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and enforcement of minimum requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Circular A-76 guidelines, whoever wins the bid is to provide the actual minimum requirements of the Government. Fort Sill defined the minimum requirement as the level of work done by its in-house employees before the cost study.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The solicitation and contract must clearly define the minimum performance standard (the in-house baseline) and the contractor is required to meet it; performance below that standard is noncompliant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of the conversion differential
rubrics_metrics.description: OMB Cost Comparison Handbook: the conversion differential is to take into account factors such as the loss of production, the temporary decrease in efficiency and effectiveness, and the cost of retained grade and pay for the displaced federal employees when converting to contract from an in-house operation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: GAO treated the conversion differential as a potential expense to the agency and deducted it from savings; DoD disputed this, asserting the conversion differential is a decision threshold (minimum savings required) not an expense. Reports and decisions should document how the conversion differential is treated and justify that approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Award-fee plan must motivate excellence (not reward minimum performance)
rubrics_metrics.description: The approach to paying award fees at Ft. Sill called for Northrop to be paid the entire available award fee for meeting, not exceeding, minimum performance standards and for a portion of the fee to be paid for less than minimum performance. As a result, the contractor was paid for performance that was below minimum standards and had no motivation for exceeding minimum performance standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Award-fee provisions should be structured to (1) withhold full fees for mere compliance with minimums, (2) pay fees for exceeding standards, and (3) include incentives for controlling costs. Do not construct award-fee provisions that pay maximum fees for minimum performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper award-fee design includes cost control incentive
rubrics_metrics.description: A properly structured award fee plan includes an incentive for controlling costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Award-fee plans should incorporate explicit cost-control measures so that improving performance does not automatically increase reimbursable costs; contracting officers should ensure the award-fee plan aligns performance incentives with cost containment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oversight necessary for accountability of costs and performance
rubrics_metrics.description: For accountability of costs and performance, oversight is necessary to ensure that the government gets what it contracted for. TRADOC and Army headquarters are to review solicitation packages before issuance and should follow up on instructions and problems identified during cost studies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although not always required to oversee individual contracts after award, higher-level commands should be informed of problematic solicitation approaches (e.g., unacceptable award-fee provisions) and should follow up to determine whether instructions were implemented and whether contractor performance is adequate. Establish formal oversight of cost-plus-award-fee contracts to ensure proper administration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contracting officer must not pay award fees for minimum or below-minimum performance
rubrics_metrics.description: GAO recommendation: ensure that Ft. Sill’s contracting officer stops using the current contract administration approach of paying award fees for minimum and below minimum performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contracting officers must administer award fees consistent with guidance and should revise or remove provisions that allow payment for substandard performance; follow-up actions and enforcement are required to correct improper administration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement for contractor improvement plan and remedial action
rubrics_metrics.description: GAO recommended the contracting officer require the contractor to provide, within a specific time frame, a plan that will demonstrate how it proposes to meet minimum performance standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the contractor fails to submit an acceptable plan, remedies may include intensified oversight, cure notices, and other corrective actions (GAO originally recommended possible termination but later deleted mandatory termination language to preserve flexibility). The installation should determine next steps after reviewing the plan.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performance monitoring: use of discrepancy reports and cure notices
rubrics_metrics.description: Fort Sill issued 83 discrepancy reports on Northrop's performance and had considered issuing a cure notice; instead, Fort Sill continued contractor operation with government employees assisting to correct problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain and act upon discrepancy reports; consider cure notices where appropriate and ensure that the contractor corrects deficiencies rather than allowing chronic underperformance to persist without remediation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Productivity measurement and standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Productivity measures should include timeliness, quality, and cost of performance. In the Ft. Sill case, productivity was compared to previous in-house performance (the in-house baseline) and showed Northrop averaged about 82 percent of the standard over the first 17 months.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use objective productivity metrics and compare to the in-house baseline established during the A-76 study; document components (timeliness, quality, cost) and calculate impacts (e.g., excess labor costs, projected contract cost increases, effects on equipment readiness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal controls over supply and maintenance
rubrics_metrics.description: Contractor internal controls over elements of the supply and maintenance functions must be adequate; lack of controls resulted in problems such as supply inventory errors and vehicle maintenance backlogs at Ft. Sill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate propriety of vendor payments, contract reimbursements, and contract monitoring procedures; ensure the contractor implements robust internal control systems to prevent inventory errors and backlogs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact of reduced productivity on costs and readiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Reduced productivity resulted in excess labor costs (about $1.8 million for first 17 months, projected to $4.5 million over the contract) and impaired equipment readiness (combat units supported had average readiness of 85 percent versus the previous in-house 90 percent).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When measuring contractor performance, quantify cost impacts and operational consequences (e.g., equipment readiness) and use those measures to trigger contract remedies or cost studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circular A-76 supplement: new cost study if contract costs become unreasonable
rubrics_metrics.description: The Circular A-76 supplement requires a new cost study be done if contract costs become unreasonable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If projected or realized contract costs materially exceed estimates, the installation should consider initiating a new A-76 cost study to reassess the cost-effectiveness of contracting out.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government payment rule for contractor costs
rubrics_metrics.description: The Government is required to pay only allocable, allowable, and reasonable costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contract administration and reimbursement must ensure costs billed are properly allocable to the contract, allowable under the FAR and contract terms, and reasonable in amount; contracting officers and auditors must enforce these standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Solicitation and award fee provision compliance with procurement regulations
rubrics_metrics.description: TRADOC advised Fort Sill that the proposed contract provisions for award fees were unacceptable and revisions were to conform to procurement regulations. The GAO indicated the logistics contract, as written, does not violate procurement regulations but that the administration approach was contrary to instructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Solicitation packages and award-fee provisions should be reviewed and, where necessary, revised to conform to procurement regulations and higher-headquarters guidance; ensure follow-up to confirm unacceptable solicitation language has not been reintroduced or improperly administered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of consistent criteria when comparing in-house and contractor costs
rubrics_metrics.description: The same criteria were used for both parties in the GAO review; if the number of employees or the workload requirements increased or decreased, both parties were assumed affected the same way. The only variables were labor wage rates and contract administration fees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When conducting cost comparisons, apply the same work-quantity and performance assumptions to both in-house and contractor alternatives; clearly document any differing assumptions (e.g., wage scales) and their justifications.
